alt: The collapse of Austria-Hungary in late 1918 and the loss of Ottoman Arab provinces left the peacemakers to recognise new states and draw borders. Self-determination, the right of peoples to govern themselves, sits at the centre, clashing with four other aims: rewarding allies, punishing the defeated, strategic frontiers and imperial interests.
caption: Self-determination guided the redrawing but clashed with the victors' other aims.

alt: Timeline of the five treaties: Saint-Germain with Austria (September 1919), Neuilly with Bulgaria (November 1919), Trianon with Hungary (June 1920), Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire (August 1920, never enforced) and Lausanne with Turkey (July 1923), with the main terms of each.
caption: Saint-Germain, Neuilly, Trianon, Sèvres, then Lausanne, which replaced Sèvres.

after: ## Austria: a small state with a large capital
alt: Four linked steps: Austria became a small landlocked republic with a capital built for an empire; it lost industry and markets behind new tariffs; union with Germany was forbidden, seeming to contradict self-determination; and by 1922 it needed a League of Nations loan.
caption: Too small to stand alone and forbidden to unite with Germany, Austria needed a League loan by 1922.

alt: A bar to scale shows Hungary kept about one-third of its territory and lost about two-thirds: Transylvania to Romania, Slovakia and Ruthenia to Czechoslovakia, Croatia to Yugoslavia. Cards note over three million Hungarians outside the borders, the treaty signed from weakness, the slogan "No, no, never!" and later revisionism.
caption: Losing two-thirds of its land made Trianon the most resented treaty.

after: ## The Ottoman Empire, Sèvres and the rise of Turkey
alt: Timeline from the Sykes-Picot Agreement (1916) and Balfour Declaration (1917) to the Treaty of Sèvres (1920), Kemal's victories of 1919-22 including Smyrna, the Chanak crisis (1922), the Treaty of Lausanne (July 1923) and the Turkish republic (October 1923).
caption: Kemal's victories and the Allies' unwillingness to fight replaced Sèvres with Lausanne.

alt: Table comparing the Treaty of Sèvres (1920) with the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) on Smyrna, eastern Thrace, Armenia, the Straits, reparations, the Greek-Turkish population exchange and the Arab mandates. A note explains Lausanne was the only negotiated treaty.
caption: Lausanne reversed most of Sèvres: the only treaty negotiated rather than imposed.

alt: Two columns. Strengths: new nations for Poles, Czechs, Slovaks, Romanians and South Slavs, democracies, minority treaties, a League role and a stable Greek-Turkish border. Difficulties: minorities, economic damage, weak states, Italian and Arab disappointment, and revisionism.
caption: Self-determination created new nations but left minorities and resentment everywhere.

alt: A question 1 answer on an invented 1921 Hungarian postcard: the content shows the map cut away, knowledge adds the loss of two-thirds of the land and three million Hungarians, and the provenance shows resentment was widely shared. A note says to check provenance against the treaty described.
caption: Content, precise knowledge and provenance together support the claim.
